title: “LOVE YOUR ENEMIES” SOUNDS BEAUTIFUL—UNTIL JESUS ASKS YOU TO LOVE YOURS
paragraphs:
“LOVE YOUR ENEMIES” SOUNDS BEAUTIFUL—UNTIL JESUS ASKS YOU TO LOVE YOURS
The command we quote when the enemy is imaginary becomes painfully different when the enemy has a name, a face, a history with you—and wounds you still carry.
“Love your enemies.”
Four words.
Beautiful enough for a church wall. Gentle enough for a Christian caption. Familiar enough that some of us can repeat them without even thinking.
But then Jesus allows a face to appear in your mind.
And suddenly the verse is not beautiful anymore.
It hurts.
Because your enemy is not an abstract theological category.
Your enemy may be the person who humiliated you when nobody defended you.
The friend who knew your secrets and weaponized them.
The spouse who betrayed promises made before God.
The relative who keeps reopening wounds and then acts as though nothing happened.
The person who lied about you.
The person who damaged your reputation.
The person who never apologized.
The person who apologized—and somehow did it again.
Maybe even the person who sits in church, raises their hands during worship, speaks about Jesus publicly, and still knows exactly what they did to you.
Now read Christ’s words again.
“But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you…”
—Matthew 5:44, KJV
In the Greek text, the heart of the command is startlingly direct:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν
egō de legō hymin, agapate tous echthrous hymōn
“But I say to you, love your enemies.”
That word ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate comes from ἀγαπάω — agapaō, the verb commonly translated “to love.”
And notice something important.
Jesus did not say, “Pretend they never hurt you.”
He did not say, “Call evil good.”
He did not say, “Trust everyone who betrayed you.”
He did not say, “Remain where someone can continue abusing you.”
He did not say forgiveness eliminates wisdom, justice, consequences, boundaries, or accountability.
He said:
Love them.
And perhaps that is harder.
Because biblical enemy-love does not require you to manufacture warm feelings toward evil.
It requires something deeper.
It requires surrendering your supposed right to become evil because evil was done to you.
That is where this command finds us.
Not in sentiment.
In the war happening inside the wounded heart.
There is a version of revenge that never throws a punch.
It simply keeps the courtroom open.
Every morning.
Every night.
Every time their name appears.
Every time somebody mentions what happened.
The evidence is presented again.
The prosecution begins again.
The sentence is pronounced again.
And somewhere deep inside, you may imagine a future scene where they finally understand how badly they hurt you.
Maybe they lose something.
Maybe their lies are exposed.
Maybe everyone finally discovers that you were telling the truth.
Maybe they come crawling back.
And you tell yourself:
“I don't hate them. I just want justice.”
Sometimes that may genuinely be true.
Justice matters to God.
But sometimes underneath our language about justice is something darker:
“I need them to hurt before I can heal.”
And Jesus puts His finger directly there.
Because if another person's suffering becomes the price of your peace, they still control you.
Read that again.
If their destruction is necessary for your healing, your heart is still chained to what they did.
Jesus offers another way.
Not denial.
Not weakness.
Not pretending.
Freedom.
Luke records Jesus saying:
“But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.”
—Luke 6:27–28, KJV
Pray for them.
That sounds almost offensive when the wound is fresh.
“Jesus, You know what they did.”
Pray for them.
“But they haven't apologized.”
Pray for them.
“They're telling people I was the problem.”
Pray for them.
“They seem happy after destroying me.”
Pray for them.
“But Lord…”
And perhaps beneath all our objections is the terrifying realization that Jesus is not merely trying to change our enemy.
He is refusing to let hatred change us.
That does not mean every relationship must be restored to what it was.
Reconciliation and forgiveness are related, but they are not identical.

Forgiveness can be extended from a heart surrendered to God even when reconciliation is presently impossible. Healthy reconciliation ordinarily requires truth, repentance, and a willingness to rebuild what was broken. Trust can take time to restore. Some situations require strong boundaries. Serious wrongdoing may require involvement from church leadership, professionals, authorities, or law enforcement.
Christian forgiveness is not permission for another person to continue harming you.
Jesus never commanded His followers to rename darkness “light.”
He commands something more radical:
Do not let darkness recruit you.
And now the command becomes frighteningly personal.
Because perhaps you have never struck your enemy.
But you have rehearsed arguments against them in the shower.
Perhaps you have never publicly cursed them.
But secretly you enjoy hearing that life is going badly for them.
Perhaps you would never call it revenge.
You simply hope God “teaches them a lesson.”
And strangely, the lesson in your imagination always looks suspiciously like suffering.
This is why loving enemies is harder than we think.
The enemy is not only standing outside us.
Something inside us wants permission to hate.
And Jesus refuses to give it.
There is an ancient command behind His teaching.
Leviticus 19:18 says:
“Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
The Hebrew expression for “you shall love your neighbor” is:
וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ
ve'ahavta lere'akha kamokha
“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Notice what comes immediately around that command.
No vengeance.
No grudge.
Love.
God knew thousands of years ago what resentment does to the human soul.
A grudge feels like protection because it tells you, “If I stay angry enough, nobody can hurt me like that again.”
But resentment cannot travel alone.
You carry it.

And eventually the person who wounded you can be absent from the room while the wound still dictates your emotions, your relationships, your reactions, your sleep, your prayers, and sometimes even your view of God.
They hurt you once.
Bitterness keeps replaying it.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than religious vocabulary.
Because Christianity does not begin with good people learning to tolerate bad people.
It begins with guilty people being reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Paul writes:
—Romans 5:10, KJV
Did you catch that word?
Enemies.
Before Christianity asks you to think about the person who became your enemy, it confronts you with the God against whom sin placed you in rebellion.
That changes everything.
We naturally divide humanity into categories.
Victim and offender.
Good person and bad person.
Me and them.
Then we come to the cross.
And the ground becomes level.
This does not erase the moral difference between someone who was wronged and someone who committed the wrong. Scripture does not require us to pretend every human action is equally evil.
But before God, none of us can boast of our own righteousness.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
You may not have committed their sin.
But you need the same Savior.
You may not carry their particular guilt.
But you still stand before God by grace.
And suddenly Jesus' command becomes inseparable from Jesus' cross.
Because what did Christ do while His enemies crucified Him?
Luke 23:34 records:
“Father, forgive them…”
Think about the scene.
Nails.
Mockery.
Blood.
Humiliation.
Injustice.
And Jesus prays.
This is not sentimental Christianity.
This is enemy-love bleeding.
The cross reveals that divine love does not wait for its enemies to become lovable before moving toward mercy.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we deserved another chance.
Not after humanity proved itself worthy.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
This is why loving your enemy is impossible to understand if Christianity becomes merely a system for becoming nicer.
You cannot manufacture Calvary from human willpower.
Enemy-love is Gospel fruit.
We love because we have encountered a love we could never deserve.
We forgive because we know what it means to need forgiveness.
We surrender vengeance because final judgment belongs to God.
Paul writes:
—Romans 12:19, KJV
That verse does not say evil does not matter.
It says evil matters so much that judgment belongs in hands more righteous than yours.
Forgiveness is not saying:
“They got away with it.”
Forgiveness says:
“I am removing myself from God's throne.”
There is a difference.
You can tell God exactly what happened.
You can grieve.
You can seek justice through appropriate means.
You can establish boundaries.
You can refuse to participate in manipulation.
You can say, “What happened was wrong.”
And still pray:
“Jesus, I surrender vengeance to You.”
Sometimes forgiveness begins there.
Not with a feeling.
With surrender.
“Lord, I don't want to forgive them.”
That may be one of the most honest prayers you have ever prayed.
“Lord, part of me wants them to hurt.”
Keep going.
“Lord, I keep replaying it.”
Keep going.
“Lord, when I see them, anger comes back.”
Keep going.
“Lord, I cannot change my own heart.”
Now you are getting close to the place grace does its deepest work.
Because Christianity was never about impressing God with your ability to repair yourself.
Bring Him the ugly truth.
Bring Him the rage.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the fantasy of revenge.
Bring Him the tears you stopped explaining because nobody seemed to understand.
Bring Him the memory you cannot erase.
Jesus already knows.
And ask Him to do something terrifying:
“Make my heart look more like Yours.”
Maybe you cannot pray, “Lord, bless them,” yet without feeling dishonest.
Begin smaller.
“Lord, I give them to You.”
Tomorrow:
“Lord, keep me from hatred.”
Later:
“Lord, bring them to repentance.”
And perhaps eventually:
“Lord, save them. Heal what is broken in them. Bring them completely to Christ.”
Do you realize what just happened?
You stopped praying for their destruction.
You started praying for their redemption.
That is warfare.
Imagine the person who wounded you genuinely encountering Jesus.
Not pretending.
Not escaping consequences.
Not using Christianity as a costume.
Imagine them broken over their sin, confessing it before God, turning from it, receiving mercy through Christ, and becoming a completely different person.
Would that anger you?
Be honest.
Because sometimes we want Jesus to forgive sinners in theory.
We just don't want Him forgiving that one.
But grace is scandalous precisely because nobody can purchase it with deserving.
The thief on the cross could not repair his reputation.
Peter could not un-deny Jesus.
Paul could not resurrect the Christians whose persecution he had supported.
And you cannot travel backward and erase your worst moments.
Yet Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
This is our scandal.
And this is our grace.
He rewrites persecutors into apostles.
He rewrites failures into witnesses.
He rewrites shame into testimony.
He rewrites enemies into family.
And sometimes the story He wants to rewrite is not the story of the person who hurt you first.
Sometimes He begins with what their hurt has been turning you into.
That is difficult to hear.
Because pain can become identity.
We can become so accustomed to telling the story of what they did that we no longer know who we would be without the wound.
Jesus does.
You are not being called to forget your story.
You are being invited to stop letting your enemy write its ending.
Christ gets the final sentence.
Maybe you are reading this with tears nobody can see.
Maybe one particular name has followed you through almost every paragraph.
Don't run from it.
Bring that name before Jesus.
You don't need to post the person's name publicly. You don't need to expose private details.
But you can be honest about your own heart.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer struggling to obey this command.
That matters.
Sharing Christian content does not earn salvation.
Buying something does not make God love you more.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation is by God's grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But if Christ has given us truth, we should want truth to travel.
Send it privately to the believer who told you, “I want to forgive, but I don't know how.”
Save it too.
Because forgiving an enemy is rarely a one-time emotional moment.
Sometimes tomorrow morning the memory returns.
Sometimes next month their name appears.
Sometimes you need to come back and remember:
Forgiveness does not mean evil was acceptable.
It means evil will not become your master.
One meaningful way to glorify God with what He has entrusted to us is to support faithful Gospel work and help biblical truth reach others.
And don't keep the invitation to yourself.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend quietly losing faith.
Invite the believer who feels spiritually numb.
Invite the seeker with difficult questions.
Invite the Christian who has slowly become comfortable living far from God.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to be good.
Let them discover grace.
Look at your own heart.
Because the most dangerous enemy may not be the person who wounded you.
It may be the bitterness asking permission to become part of you.
Jesus is calling you somewhere better.
To repentance.
To grace.
To forgiveness.
To freedom.
To the cross.
And perhaps tonight you finally need to say:

“Jesus, what they did was wrong. You know how deeply it hurt. I cannot rewrite yesterday. I cannot force them to repent. I cannot manufacture feelings I do not have. But I surrender my right to revenge. Judge rightly. Protect what needs protecting. Heal what has been wounded. Forgive my own sin. Teach me to pray for those who hurt me. Keep bitterness from becoming my identity. Make me more like You.”
That prayer does not make the wound imaginary.
It means the wound no longer gets to be your god.
The scars may remain.
But scars are not always evidence that the story ended in destruction.
Sometimes scars are evidence that the wound did not win.
Look at the risen Jesus.
He still bore scars.
Yet death no longer owned Him.
And because He lives, your pain does not have to write the final chapter either.
Your enemy may have written one of the darkest pages of your life—but they do not hold the pen that writes your ending. Jesus does.
